strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine label noise in preference datasets with clear empirical evidence (20-40% corruption rates)
Elegant theoretical framework connecting arbitrary preference losses to probabilistic models via Gibbs distribution, enabling generalization across multiple algorithms (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 algorithms, 2 models, multiple datasets (UltraFeedback, MultiPref), and benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard)
Consistent empirical improvements (3-7% win rate gains) across all tested configurations, not cherry-picked results
Solid theoretical contribution with Theorem 4.1 providing convergence guarantees and verification through controlled synthetic noise experiments
Practical implementation with clear Algorithm 1, runtime overhead analysis (11% average slowdown), and reproducibility resources provided
Thorough ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis demonstrating robustness
Qualitative analysis showing RE-PO identifies genuinely noisy/reversed preference labels in real datasets
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.1 assumes perfectly calibrated model and full-batch EM, but implementation uses mini-batch gradient updates with EMA (Generalized EM). Theoretical guarantees don't cover the actual algorithm used.

Limited novelty of core technique: EM for noisy labels (Dawid-Skene 1979, Crowd-BT 2013) is well-established. Main contribution is applying existing methods to preference learning, which is somewhat incremental.
No human evaluation despite alignment work targeting human preferences. Automatic LLM-based evaluators (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard) can be biased and don't directly measure alignment quality.

Experimental limitations: Main results treat UltraFeedback as single virtual annotator (K=1), limiting leverage of multi-annotator EM. MultiPref improvements (3-4% LC) substantially weaker than UltraFeedback (4-7% LC).
Hyperparameter sensitivity: Performance highly sensitive to EMA parameter α (30.1% at α=0.001 vs 35.5% at α=0.1). No principled guidance for setting η₀ and α on new datasets.

Synthetic noise experiments (Section 5.5) use uniform noise on small calibrated model, but real preference noise is typically systematic (annotator bias, instruction ambiguity). Gap between verification conditions and real-world applicability.

Theory requires 'perfectly calibrated model' assumption. While paper starts from instruction-tuned LLMs, it acknowledges failure mode if base model is misaligned—this is a significant practical limitation not thoroughly validated.
Limited model scope: Experiments only on 7-8B scale. Generalization to larger/smaller models unclear. Unclear how method performs on model families beyond Mistral/Llama.
Incomplete baseline comparisons: No direct empirical comparison with Selective DPO (mentioned but not evaluated). Mixed results vs. rDPO/Hölder-DPO on some configurations.
Missing analysis of noise characterization: No systematic study of which noise types RE-PO handles best/worst. Limited error analysis or investigation of when confidence scores fail.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real label noise (20-40% corruption) in preference datasets
Principled EM-based approach grounded in established crowdsourcing theory (Dawid-Skene, Crowd-BT)
Elegant generalization connecting arbitrary preference losses to probabilistic models via Gibbs distribution (Eq. 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B), datasets (UltraFeedback, MultiPref), and methods (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO)
Consistent improvements across configurations (4-7pp on AlpacaEval 2)
Empirical verification of theoretical claims through controlled synthetic noise experiments (Section 5.5)
Ablation studies analyzing hyperparameter sensitivity (Section 5.4)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core EM-based technique for noisy labels is from Dawid-Skene (1979) and Crowd-BT (2013); application to LLM alignment is incremental

Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.1 assumes perfect calibration (unrealistic early in training) and full-batch EM, while Algorithm 1 uses mini-batch training with EMA; convergence properties of the practical algorithm are not analyzed

Multi-annotator handling undermined: main experiments (Table 2) treat all UltraFeedback data as K=1 single virtual annotator, contradicting claimed capabilities; MultiPref experiments feel like an afterthought

Modest improvements without statistical rigor: 4-7pp gains reported without significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars; some metrics show inconsistent trends (e.g., SimPO Llama-3-8B: LC improves but WR decreases)
Limited baseline comparisons: rDPO and Hölder-DPO only shown for DPO; label smoothing baseline is conceptually different, making comparison unfair
Substantial hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 4) with unclear selection procedure; optimal values (η₀=0.9, α=0.1) appear grid-searched without justification
Non-trivial computational overhead (Table 8) of 11-40% downplayed in main text; some configurations show slowdowns exceeding 30%
Equation 2's probabilistic conversion of arbitrary losses via exp(-L_pref) lacks principled justification; different losses have different scales
Overclaimed 'general framework' status: RE-PO is a wrapper computing soft weights; extension to different losses is straightforward and not fundamentally novel
Synthetic noise experiments (Section 5.5) use tiny 0.5B model; generalization to larger models with larger theory-practice gaps is unclear
Qualitative analysis anecdotal (Appendix F): only 2 cherry-picked low-confidence examples; systematic analysis of identified noisy patterns lacking
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability statement; some implementation details unclear; baseline hyperparameters not fully specified
Missing statistical significance testing and characterization of when RE-PO provides most benefit

strengths: Addresses a critical practical problem: label noise in preference datasets for LLM alignment, with well-motivated empirical evidence (20-40% corrupted labels)

Elegant generalization framework: connects arbitrary preference losses to probabilistic models via Gibbs distribution (Eq. 2), enabling systematic transformation of multiple algorithms into robust counterparts

Comprehensive experimental validation: consistent improvements across 4 algorithms, 2 base models, multiple benchmarks, real multi-annotator data, with thorough ablations and synthetic noise verification
Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.1 provides convergence guarantees for annotator reliability recovery with proof provided; Section 5.5 empirically validates theoretical claims
Practical algorithm design: Algorithm 1 clearly specified with acceptable ~11% computational overhead; EMA updates enable efficient mini-batch training
Strong empirical results: up to 7.0% win rate improvements on AlpacaEval 2, consistent gains across diverse configurations, qualitative analysis identifying genuinely noisy labels
High reproducibility: algorithm details, hyperparameters, runtime measurements provided; resources linked in appendix
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.1 assumes perfect calibration (unrealistic in practice); practical algorithm uses mini-batch Generalized EM without convergence guarantees, yet theory only applies to idealized full-batch setting
Limited analysis of failure modes: paper acknowledges that highly misaligned initialization could cause RE-PO to fail, but provides no experiments, detection strategies, or practical remedies
Considerable hyperparameter sensitivity: arena-hard WR ranges 12.9-14.7 across α values (13% variance); insufficient guidance for practitioners to set η₀ and α without extensive ablation
Modest improvements in some configurations: several results show only 1-3% gains (e.g., SimPO on Llama-3-8B: 48.1 vs 46.9); MultiPref results are more variable than main experiments
Incomplete robustness baseline comparisons: limited comparison with rDPO and Hölder-DPO; no comparison with other noise-robust learning methods (co-training, mixup, etc.)

Single virtual annotator assumption: main experiments treat diverse annotators as K=1, limiting demonstration of the framework's multi-annotator modeling strength; full advantage only shown on MultiPref
Limited noise characterization: insufficient analysis of which noise types RE-PO handles well/poorly; unclear if gains come from noise removal vs. label-smoothing regularization effects

Evaluation methodology concerns: heavy reliance on automatic evaluation (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard); no human evaluation; Arena-Hard gains substantially smaller than AlpacaEval 2, suggesting possible benchmark artifacts
Incremental core novelty: EM approach builds directly on established Dawid-Skene and Crowd-BT models; main contribution is systematic application to modern alignment via probabilistic connection
Missing critical ablations: no analysis of whether simpler per-sample confidence weighting suffices; no experiments with severely misaligned base models; limited sensitivity analysis on η₀ range

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine label noise (20-40%) in preference alignment datasets with clear practical impact
Principled EM-based approach with mathematical rigor; Theorem 4.1 provides convergence guarantees for annotator reliability recovery
Elegant Gibbs construction (Eq. 2) generalizing framework across diverse preference losses (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO)
Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple algorithms, models (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B), datasets (UltraFeedback, MultiPref), and benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard)
Consistent improvements across configurations (up to 7.0% on AlpacaEval 2 LC) demonstrating generality
Strong reproducibility: detailed algorithms, proofs, controlled synthetic noise verification (Figure 2), qualitative analysis of identified noisy labels
Practical implementation with measured overhead (~11% average) and hyperparameter ablations
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.1 assumes perfect calibration and full-batch updates; practical implementation uses mini-batch Generalized EM (Eq. 7). Idealized assumptions don't extend to realistic setting, limiting theoretical justification
Limited algorithmic novelty: Core EM approach for unreliable annotators well-established (Dawid-Skene 1979); contribution is primarily application to LLM alignment rather than new techniques

Mixed empirical results with high variance by configuration: SimPO degrades on Llama WR (37.1→39.4 only), label smoothing achieves comparable performance (SimPO: 48.1 vs RE-SimPO: 46.9), no statistical significance testing

Surprisingly strong label smoothing baselines make it unclear whether EM-based approach is fundamentally better; insufficient analysis of relationship between methods and computational overhead justification (11-40%)

Limited exploration of failure modes and method applicability: no systematic analysis of when RE-PO underperforms, when to apply vs. simpler alternatives, or how to select hyperparameters (η₀, α) with unknown noise

Main experiments lack realistic noise: UltraFeedback treated as single virtual annotator; MultiPref multi-annotator evaluation limited to one dataset; synthetic noise may not reflect real annotation patterns
Missing ablations on induced probability formulation (Eq. 2) and analysis of learned vs. ground-truth annotator reliabilities; unclear how method generalizes to extreme noise rates
Presentation issues: claim of 'lifting to general framework' potentially oversold (more meta-wrapper than fundamental framework); dense exposition; insufficient intuitive explanations

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine label noise (20-40% corruption) in preference datasets for LLM alignment
Principled EM-based framework grounded in classical work (Dawid & Skene, 1979) with elegant Gibbs construction generalizing across four alignment algorithms
Versatile meta-framework applying to DPO, IPO, SimPO, and CPO with consistent improvements across different backbones
Comprehensive experimental setup including main results, multi-annotator experiments (MultiPref), ablations, theoretical verification, and qualitative analysis
Thorough reproducibility including promised code, detailed appendices with derivations, and measured runtime overhead
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.1 assumes perfect calibration and full-batch training, but Algorithm 1 uses mini-batch EMA (Generalized EM). Section 5.5's empirical verification uses 0.5B model, not 7B-8B models in main experiments, raising questions about calibration transfer

Problematic experimental design: Main experiments model all preferences as from a single virtual annotator, contradicting the framework's core motivation of handling multi-annotator disagreement. In this case, learned η essentially estimates global noise rate—why not use direct noise rate estimation like rDPO?

Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals or significance tests for Table 2 results. Improvements range 1-7 points; unclear if statistically significant. Different datasets for Mistral vs. Llama complicate comparison

Incomplete baseline comparisons: rDPO and Hölder-DPO only compared on Mistral-7B (not Llama-3-8B); ROPO cited but not compared. Label smoothing sometimes performs comparably (SimPO w/ LS achieves 48.1 LC vs. RE-SimPO's 46.9 on Llama)
Inconsistent improvements across algorithms: RE-DPO shows +7.0/+4.4 on Mistral-7B but RE-IPO only +2.1/+2.5, RE-SimPO +2.1/+3.2, RE-CPO +1.3/+1.4. Paper provides no explanation for this variation

Limited algorithmic novelty: Core contribution (EM for unreliable annotators) is classical (Dawid & Skene 1979). Chen et al. (2013) extended to pairwise comparisons. Application to LLM alignment is somewhat novel but incremental
No human evaluation: All results use automatic evaluators (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard). Improvements could be artifacts of the evaluator's preferences
For non-likelihood losses (IPO, SimPO, CPO), the induced objective differs from the original, but this semantic change receives minimal discussion. Why optimize induced objective instead?

Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection: Initial η₀=0.9 crucial (0.99 hurts, 0.55 hurts worse); EMA α=0.1 essential (small α too slow, large α too volatile). No guidance for practitioners or cross-dataset transfer
Non-negligible runtime overhead: 11% average, up to 32-40% for SimPO (Table 8). EMA update (Eq. 7) appears ad-hoc without principled derivation

strengths: Addresses important practical problem: 20-40% label noise in preference datasets with demonstrated impact on alignment quality
Principled EM-based approach grounded in prior work on learning from unreliable annotators (Dawid-Skene model)
General framework via Gibbs construction elegantly unifies multiple alignment algorithms (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO), enabling systematic robustification
Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple models (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B), algorithms, benchmarks, real multi-annotator dataset (MultiPref), and ablation studies
Strong and consistent empirical results: up to 7% win-rate improvements across all tested configurations on AlpacaEval 2
Theoretical analysis (Theorem 4.1) with empirical verification: demonstrates RE-PO can recover annotator reliability under idealized conditions and shows robustness to imperfect calibration
Practical mini-batch implementation with modest computational overhead (~11% average)
High-quality presentation with clear methodology, comprehensive appendices, and promises of code release for reproducibility
Qualitative analysis (Appendix F) effectively demonstrates RE-PO identifies genuinely problematic labels (off-task, reversed, inconsistent)
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.1 assumes perfect calibration, a strong assumption violated in practice. While empirical validation is provided, lack of convergence guarantees for realistically miscalibrated models limits theoretical contribution's practical relevance

Evaluation limited to automatic metrics (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard): known biases and validity concerns with LLM-based evaluators. Human evaluation on even a subset would strengthen claims about genuine performance improvements

Main experiments treat single-annotator datasets as if from one annotator due to missing annotator IDs, which undermines the multi-annotator framing and limits direct testing of per-annotator reliability learning
Notable hyperparameter sensitivity: method requires careful tuning of η₀ and α (Table 4), with significant performance variation. Limited guidance for practitioners on selecting these values

Incomplete baseline comparisons: limited comparisons with other noise-robust methods from broader learning-with-noisy-labels literature. Comparison with rDPO is somewhat unfair (rDPO requires knowing noise rate a priori)
Insufficient characterization of when RE-PO helps: no analysis of dataset properties predicting effectiveness, performance on very clean datasets, or which algorithm families benefit most
Prefers-as-noise assumption: Assumption 1 treats all disagreement as noise around single ground-truth; doesn't distinguish between legitimate preference heterogeneity and annotator error
Scalability questions insufficiently addressed: reliability estimation quality with large K unclear, behavior with new annotators at test time not discussed, maximum K tested is 227
Limited analysis of learned confidence distributions: unclear whether w_i values cluster near extremes or spread throughout [0,1], important for interpreting soft-label mechanism
Non-likelihood losses: for IPO, SimPO, CPO, the induced objective differs from original, but implications not deeply analyzed
